speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: POINT OF ORDER RAISED BY MR. MEIGHEN RESPECTING MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
A motion is made by the lion. Minister of Finance to revive the committee of Supply in the following words:
That this House will on Monday March 22nd, resolve itself into a committee to consider of a supply to be granted His Majesty.
The point taken by the right hon. leader of the opposition is that the power of the committee is exhausted by the decision which was rendered yesterday; that is to say that the committee should rise. Now, what is the effect of a similar motion when it is carried in committee of the whole? May I refer the House to No. 191 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms which reads:
If the motion "that the chairman do now leave the chair" is carried, then the business of the committee is superseded, but the original order of reference remains and it is competent for the House to resolve itself again into committee on the same subject, for the committee itself has no power to extinguish a question.
This is taken from Bourinot at page 400. The right hon. gentleman has quoted from May at page 538. Before coming to the point which be makes, I wish to call his attention to May's 13th edition, page 455.
It is the practice for members who desire to close the sitting of a committee, to move that the "chairman do report progress, and ask leave to sit again," in order to put an end to the proceedings of the committee on that day, this mot-ion in committee, being analogous to that frequently made at other times for adjourning the debate. A motion "That the chairman do now leave the chair" when carried, supersedes the order of the day for a committee, and converts it into a dropped order; as in this case, when the Speaker resumes the chair, no report whatever is made from the committee. The same result is obtained if, when the chairman reports progress in the matter referred to in the committee, he refrains, upon a direction given by the member who had obtained the appointment of the committee, from asking leave to sit again.
Now how can you revive a committee which has been so converted into a dropped order? May, at page 256, says:
To replace a dropped order of the day upon the notice paper, a motion is made before the commencement or after the close, of public business, to appoin. the order for a subsequent day. These motions, which are made without notice, are usually treated as purely formal motions.
Is a notice of motion necessary? Let me refer to Redlich, volume 2, page 219, where I find the following:
Certain motions of a formal or uncontentious natur* do not require notice; such are motions:
(a)	For the first reading of a bill from the House of Lords;
fSir Henry Drayton.]
(b)	For the consideration of Lords' amendments forthwith or on a future day;
(c)	For the postponement, discharge, or revival of an order of the day;
(d)	For the appointment of a committee of the whole House on a future day.
Therefore no notice is required in the present instance. I would also quote rule 76 cf our own rules and I also refer to May, page 237, where I find the following:
Certain formal motions which are necessary for the due transaction of business are also -made without notice, before the commencement, or after the close of public business, such as motions for the first reading of -bills received from the House of Lords for the consideration of Lords' amendments forthwith or upon a future day for the postponement, the discharge, or the revival of an order of the day.
I	now come to the very serious argument based on the citation made by the right hon. gentleman at page 538 of May. Let me read it again:
When all the supplies for the service of the year have been granted, the sittings of the committee of Supply are discontinued. Care must be taken not to close the committee until all the necessary grants ha/e been obtained. If the committee of Supply be designedly closed, it cannot be reopened save by the demand from the crown for further supplies made by a second Speech from the Throne, or a royal message, or by the communication of additional estimates.
My knowledge of the English language is far from perfect, but reading carefully this paragraph and using my common sense, it means that once all the supplies have been passed by the committee of Supply, then designedly the committee is closed, and if the government have further supplies to present to the House they must present them by either a second Speech from the Throne or a royal message. That is what happens every session in this House. When the bulk of the supplies have been passed, a message comes from His Excellency for further supplementary estimates and the Speaker reads the message to the House. Again, I am of the opinion, with my poor knowledge of the English language that "designedly" means that when certainly and finally the House has closed the committee all the supplies having been passed. Now, if further supplies are presented the government cannot refer them to the committee of Supply without a new message from His Excellency. That is how I read this passage of May at page 538.
The right hon. gentleman referred to the foot-notes on page 538 of May. I may say that I have taken great pains to look over the foot-notes and references and they apply simply to cases where all the main supplies have been passed and the government in England wanted to submit some further sup-

Some doubt has been expressed but it will be cleared up by this motion if it is adopted, as to whether or not the particular resolution under consideration at the time that the committee rose without report, was automatically superseded and whether or not it could be again considered by the committee without being again referred to the committee by the House. Now that hon. members are all in attendance and the Liberal members are not attending the sitting of the Customs committee nor on their way home for their evening meal, I introduce this motion so that the House may decide that the matter which was taken out of its hands yesterday shall be restored and considered. I think it is
important that there should be no misunderstanding of the exact significance of what transpired yesterday. As hon. members know' very well, when the House is in committee hon. gentlemen frequently attend to other matters than the questions immediately under consideration in this chamber, especially when they have reason to expect that a debate will go on without a division. It so happened that yesterday afternoon there was an important meeting of the committee which is investigating the smuggling charges and a large number of hon. members from this side of the House, as well as some hon. gentlemen opposite, attended that meeting. The fact that the total vote in committee in this chamber was 105 shows that one-half of the members were not in the House at the time that the vote was taken. I came into the chamber about a quarter to six, having previously been in conference in my own room with some hon. members, and at about ten minutes to six I heard my hon. friend the member for West York suggesting to the Minister of Customs that the item be not pressed at that particular moment. The Minister of Customs was replying to the effect that there were strong reasons why the item should not be held over, and I believe what he had in mind was that it was desirable to proceed with the business of the House as expeditiously as possible. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), while the Minister of Customs was speaking, kept his eye steadily on the clock, and when it was nearly six o'clock-about five minutes to six-instead of making any motion of any kind respecting the item, either to strike it out or to reduce it, he moved to have the committee rise at once in order, so he said, to show his good faith in the whole matter. No Prime Minister has ever met the House of Commons in circumstances similar to those in which I meet it. For the time being no party in this House has a majority. I think that we will have less to say about party and less to think about party than we have had hitherto, and that we shall lay more and more emphasis upon the responsibility of individual members of this House of voting as responsible members of the House and not merely as party politicians. I have known an adjoining building, where there happens to be a convenient division bell, used for similar purposes. I have seen the House, practically empty when the bells began to ring, suddenly transformed into a very riotous sort of market-place by the inrush of members, doing their best for their nation, for the House of Commons and for their party, to find a government napping, and to turn it out upon a stupid issue.

Search for the bodies of the Phipps family, held beneath the ice of lake Erie, was definitely abandoned Wednesday. No further effective measures for their discovery can be taken until the lake is clear of ice.

Mr. Ford has decided not to communicate with the Ontario Hydro Commission with regard to the use of electrical devices. He believes electricity would not be effective through the ice.

Thank you. This letter is from Leamington, Ontario, under date of March 6, although it was not received by me until Monday of this week. It is as follows:
Since the accident here last Monday, in the casualty list were included a man by the name of James Phipps, his wife, and three children between three and ten years of age, who took a plunge through the ice somewhere between Pelee island and Leamington in a closed Ford sedan. The present situation is a crime against the people of the mainland and the island. Something surely must be done. The island has been cut off from the mainland this winter and isolated on account of a broken cable, and there has been no communication whatsoever with the mainland. This service between two sections of Canada lying within fourteen miles of each other is so deplorable as to be pathetic. The ill-fated party and car lay on the bottom of lake Erie from Monday afternoon until Thursday before the fatality was discovered. Both terminals were unconscious of what had transpired, the island supposing the party had landed safely, and the mainland content to think they had remained on the island, whereas they were resting beneath the ice and waters of lake Erie.
It is worth while for the government to think it over. Five human lives were lost in one dive, which is too many to go on record. The island is in dire need of assistance, and I should like to ask the government if, in

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to approve of the agreement dated the sixth day of July, 1925, between the government of the Dominion of Canada and the governments of certain of His Majesty's colonies in the West Indies, which agreement is termed "Canada-British West Indies-Bermuda-British Guiana-British Honduras Trade Agreement, 1925," and to provide:
1.	That after the said agreement is brought into force, and so long as it remains in force, goods mentioned in the said agreement, the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies parties to the said agreement, which are conveyed without transshipment, except transshipment at a port of any of the said colonies, by ship direct into a sea or river port of Canada, shall be admitted to Canada at the rates of duties provided in the said agreement.
2.	That the tariff concessions covered by the said agreement to be extended to goods the produce or manufacture of any of the said colonies shall be so extended with respect to any one or more of the said colonies which may have ratified the said agreement on and after a day to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council, which proclamation shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
3.	That subject to the provisions of the Customs Tariff, 1907, the Governor in Council may, by order in council, extend the said advantages to goods the produce or manufacture of any British country.
4.	That the operation of all laws inconsistent with the giving to the provisions of the said agreement and of any act that may be founded on thi3 resolution their full effect shall from time to time be suspended to the extent of such inconsistencies.
5.	That subject to the ratification of the said agreement by the various colonies which are parties thereto, and to the fulfilment of their undertaking to make the contributions on their behalf as specified therein, the Governor in Council be empowered to make such arrangements as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the said agreement relating to the establishment of steamship services between Canada and the colonies concerned, and any expenses incurred in carrying out the said agreement shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for that purpose.
He said: Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on the record some of the provisions of the agreement, and to give a brief history of the negotiations carried on from year to year between Canada and the islands of the West Indies. The West Indies islands represented in this agreement
have a population of roughly 2,200,000 persons, as compared with a population of 1,218,913 in New Zealand and 5,435,734 in Australia, according to the last census.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How is that divided?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not tell my hon. friend; I have not the details. The government of Canada, or rather the people of Canada, have recognized for many years the importance of trade relations with the West Indies. This agreement which will be submitted to parliament is one of a series of agreements which have been made from year to year. Thirty-five years ago, in 1890, the government of the day sent to the West India islands Sir George Foster, then Minister of Finance, in an attempt to arrange commercial reciprocity between Canada and the British West Indies. No results crowned his efforts, for at that time the West India governments were negotiating with the United States for a favourable treatment under the McKinley Tariff Act, and they thought that if they granted a reciprocal preference to Canada, the United States would penalize West Indian sugar, one of the great products of the West India islands, and the main product of the colonies at that time. In 1897, seven years later, a royal commission investigated conditions in the West Indies, and reported that the views of the West Indies estate proprietors remained unchanged. In 1896 there was a change of government in Canada. In 1898 Mr. Fielding extended to the British West Indies the Canadian preferential tariff, and in the course of his budget statement pointed out the large opportunities that existed for the development of trade between Canada and those islands. Accepting Canada's imperial responsibilities Mr. Fielding then extended the preference without asking for any concessions in return. In 1900 the preferential reduction on British imports into Canada was increased from 25 per cent to 33i per cent, but our trade with the West India islands still remained at a low level. The same year however, Trinidad sent delegates to Ottawa, and as a result the Canadian government made a proposal to the Trinidad government for a reciprocal trade arrangement. This failed to materialize into legislation. Apparently the people of Trinidad were not prepared to grant to Canada the preferences which we desired.
In 1903 the Brussels convention, brought the West Indian sugar question again to the fore. This convention, which aimed at the abolition of the bounties on the production of sugar brought in its train the disappearance of
172b

Canada-West Indies Agreement
the American countervailing duties on bounty-fed sugar, and made the American market less attractive to the West Indian growers. In the same year Canada imposed a surtax on German importation into our country.
By 1903 the Spanish-American war had ended, and the effect of Porto Rico becoming a part of the United Sia'es was felt, because sugar from that country was imported into the United States free of duty, and a similar treatment was extended t*o importations from the Philippines and r reduction of 20 per cent to those of Cuba. This practically ended, for the moment, the export of sugar from the British West Indies to the United States. These three circumstances influenced the desire to commence fresh negotiations between Canada and the West Indies which later on brought about a measure of trade agreement with the West India islands. Negotiations were opened between Canada and the West Indies and British Guiana, including proposals for a reduction of 10 per cent on importations from Canada and the United Kingdom. Likewise in 1904 Trinidad revived the proposals of 1900. The proposals which Trinidad had rejected in 1900 they were prepared, apparently, in 1904 to accept.
I said a moment ago that all Canadian governments had been anxious to effect commercial relations with the British West Indies. In so doing these governments were only representing the views of the people, because we find that in 1907 the boards of trade of Toronto, Montreal, St. John, and Halifax sent a commission to the West Indies to study trade conditions. In that year the groundwork was laid for the holding of a conference at Barbados in 1908 to consider the steps which might be taken to encourage closer trade relations with Canada. This conference was held in January, 1908. Canada was represented by two delegates, and practically all the colonies were represented. The representatives, however, had no power to bind their governments, and only a general exchange of views was possible. The Canadian government, realizing the difficulties involved in the conclusion of separate reciprocal agreements with each of the colonies, proposed that a conference organized by imperial authority should take place. Accordingly in 1909 a commission was appointed by Great Britain, headed by Lord Balfour of Burleigh, who was chairman of that commission. The commission, I am told, consisted of five members. The Canadian representatives on that royal commission were tne Hon. W. S. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, and the Hon. William Paterson, then Minister of Customs. This commission visited the principal cities

of eastern Canada. Later all the members excepting Mr. Fielding visited the West India islands. During the same year the commission met in London, England, and drafted a report which was presented to the King's Most Excellent Majesty". A suggested form of agreement was presented with this report. The visit of the royal commission was not without results, because we find that in 1912 the first West India conference was held in Ottawa. In that year representatives from most of the islands and British Guiana visited Canada, and an agreement was entered into, the terms of which were practically the same as those of the suggested agreement of the West India commission of 1909.
The conference which took place in 1912 at Ottawa granted special tariff reductions on a few selected West Indian products, including sugar, and in addition a preferential rate of four-fifths of the general tariff on some other goods. The Canadian statute ratifying the new pact left the British West Indies in enjoy'ment of the regular British preferential schedule in any cases where it should happen to be more favourable to them than the new treaty preference. The agreement secured for Canada a corresponding preference of one-fifth of the ordinary duty in Trinidad, British Guiana, Barbados, Grenada, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Antigua, St. Kitts, Nevis, Dominica, and Montserrat on various food products, animals, boots and shoes, machinery, vehicles, soap, cement, calcium, carbide, furniture, lumber-in all, articles specified under forty-seven tariff headings. On Hour the preference was to be not less than 12 cents per hundred pounds.
In 1920 another conference was held and at this conference Jamaica, the Bahamas, British Honduras and Bermuda joined in the discussion. These four colonies had not been members of the 1912 conference, and all with the exception of Bermuda later on ratified the agreement. The act of parliament bringing the latter agreement into effect was assented to on May 3. 1921. I imagine my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was then the Prime Minister of Canada. The act provided that the agreement should come into force on a day fixed by proclamation by the Governor in Council, which was made on the 18th June, 1921. It was provided that the agreement should remain in force for ten years from the date of the proclamation and thereafter until terminated by twelve months' notice given either by the government of Canada or by the government of any of the colonies. This agreement is still in force.
The 1920 agreement was more general than the agreement of 1912.

The British West Indies lie considerably to the south of Canada. Their products are those of a tropical climate and do not enter into competition with our agricultural products. Canadian agriculture, the fishing and lumbering industries and dairying especially, together with certain branches of manufacturing, stand to gain materially from the new pact, whilst such West Indian products as bananas, sugar, molasses, coffee, cocoa and citrus fruits will either enter Canada duty free or be admitted under a lower rate than similar products from foreign countries.
The preferences granted Canada are divided into two classes, special and general. The special preferences apply to a selected list of products in which Canada is especially interested, and are greater than the general preferences. The latter apply to all goods not receiving special preferences. For example, Trinidad, Barbados and British Guiana agree under the general preference to charge practically all imports from Canada only half, British Honduras, Leeward and Windward islands two-thirds and Jamaica three-quarters of the duty levied on goods from foreign countries.
As regards special preferences, the western group of colonies consisting of Jamaica, the Bahamas, and British Honduras impose a duty on Canadian flour of two shillings a barrel less than on foreign flour and duties of not more than half those charged foreign countries on butter, cheese, lard, condensed milk, fish, apples and potatoes. In the eastern group of colonies, British Guiana, Trinidad, Barbados and other West Indian colonies also give Canada a preference of two shillings a barrel on flour and a preference of not less than 66j per cent on apples, pork, beef, lard, butter, cheese, fish, condensed milk, boards, planks, scantlings, shingles and lath, cement, prepared cocoa, confectionery, boots and shoes and cordage. It is also provided that on these items the preference shall not be less than a fixed amount.
Turning for a moment to navigation, it is admitted that the key to a successful trade with the West Indies lies in satisfactory steamship service between the colonies and Canada.
Previous to 1900, a subsidized steamship service between Canada and the West Indies was being performed by Messrs. Pickford and Black of Halifax. This subsidy was for $63,000 annually. The service was continued under a year to year arrangement until 1900, when the British government undertook to pay half the cost of the steamship service and a new contract was made with Messrs. Pickford and Black whereby they received $65,700 from Canada and a like amount from the British government. They were to maintain a fortnightly service, the vessels starting alternately from St. John and Halifax. This agreement was for five years. Towards the end of the period of the contract, the British government signified that it was not altogether satisfied with the service, the desire being to have a fast through service to Barbados, Trinidad and British Guiana, which would be supplemented by a service of slow cargo boats. Negotiations were opened with other companies but the Pickford and Black company received the contract for a twelve-day service. This was carried on until 1911, when the British government declared that it could not see its way to continue paying its portion of a subsidy based on the old ar-langement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one necessarily approaches any treaty made by this administration with considerable apprehension. They have had the treaty-making mania ever since they came into office, and never seem satisfied if three months are allowed to go by without a new excursion to the Orient or to Australia-always by the longest route-with some kind of treaty brought back as return cargo. Those so far presented in their four years of office have been a succession of unredeemed disasters. The treaty with France, the treaty with Belgium, the treaty with Australia-and fall emphatically into that category. Our trade with each of those countries has been sensibly injured, and in at least two cases very seriously so.
The present is an attempt to negotiate a treaty with the West India Islands. Had one confidence in the judgment and care and in the grasp of Canadian trade conditions of the government of the day, he would naturally welcome the negotiating of a treaty with any of our British dominions, and he would be more disposed to welcome the negotiating of

a treaty with those dominions whose trade is complementary to our own, rather than competitive therewith; and of all portions of this empire which could correctly be so described, perhaps the most conspicuous would be the West India Islands. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is entirely right when he says these islands are producing goods which this country requires but which, on account of climatic and soil conditions, it cannot very well produce. The converse applies:	our
products the West India people require, and we have a surplus with which to supply them. This no doubt accounts for the fact that over a considerable period of years and throughout a succession of governments efforts have been made to improve trade relations with those islands,-efforts which have continued in progressive degree and, I think it may be said, always with increasing success.
There are other reasons which have induced governments of the past to make these attempts; they are of what one would call an imperial character-if that adjective has not become wholly offensive to some hon. gentlemen of this House. The British West Indies are fellow-citizens of this empire with ourselves; they have been so over a long period of years; they are well thought of within the circle of the empire by all its people; and because of their position, because of their possessions and because of their history, they are entitled to the best of consideration at the hands of the rest of us; and they are able to give us something in return for the consideration we give them. Besides, they occupy a position analogous to no other portion of the empire save ourselves with relation to the United States of America. Their trade necessarily is very much influenced by the neighbourhood erf the great republic and by the trade policy of that republic. In a measure, though no part of the United States, they are subservient to America's trade policy. In corresponding measure we are the same. We, it seems to me, have a peculiar obligation with relation to those islands, and it is certainly the part of Canada to do anything within reason to enhance the interest of the people of those islands in the people of the rest of the empire, and particularly in ourselves, to add to the interest they have in our trade, to bring them, as it were, more and more within the circuit of Canadian and imperial trade rather than of American. That a like feeling prevails in the West Indies, there is no question whatever. Indeed, they view the tendency of recent times and the trade ambitions of the United States with very serious apprehensions. Their desire is to become more and more

Canada-West Indies Agreement
closely united with us and other citizens of the British Empire; and they look to us particularly, as the foremost of British dominions and the one closest to themselves, their great British neighbour on this continent, to extend to them the best trade facilities within our power.
All these considerations have had weight with administrations of the past, and they had very great weight in determining the course pursued by the late government in negotiating the treaty of 1920. That treaty has been reviewed by the Minister of Finance in his short address this afternoon. I was not one of the administration who had to do directly with the negotiation of the treaty, with its terms I am not so familiar as would be other hon. members of this House, but I have generally a fairly accurate knowledge of them. Under that treaty we secured trade preferences with the most important West India Islands of 25 to 50 per cent, that being the preference given us on their general tariff. We in turn gave them preferences equally great-indeed, greater still if I caught the words of the Minister of Finance aright when he stated that in our preferences to the West Indies the minimum was 50 per cent. We also agreed to extend to them certain steamship services, to the western group as well as to the eastern group, without which the preferences would be of little avail. This treaty has been in operation for some four years, or somewhat less than four years at the time the new treaty was made; I am not certain of the date at which it went into effect. The Minister of Finance is right in saying that as far as Canada is concerned it was ratified by this House in May, 1921, and I think the order in council supplementary to the ratification was passed, according to his words, in June. The minister is not able to say at what time it was ratified by the West Indies, but if my recollection is right the complete engagement did not take effect until some time later. Consequently the treaty was scarcely in operation at all under the late government. We were engaged in an election campaign for the last three or four months of the term of the government, and the attention which would otherwise have been given these matters of course could not be applied.
It seems that the terms of that treaty have not been wholly lived up to on the part of Canada. I was sorry indeed to learn that Canada had to make admission of having failed to live up to the terms of a solemn engagement. I do not know just what was done in the last few months of the late administration after the treaty went into effect, nor 14011-110
just how brief a period then elapsed, but I do know that no complaint was ever brought to my attention of any failure to live up to the terms of our contract. I am just informed by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) that one of the principal islands, Jamaica, if not others, did not come into the treaty at all until some time after we went out of office. Certainly there was no conscious failure to live up to the treaty during the term*of office of the last administration. I do not know just what the difficulties have been; I would like to have heard them further explained. The minister said in his remarks that both governments did the best they could. 1 fancy the obligation chiefly or wholly fell upon our successors in office, but why it was they could not do what we had engaged to do, I do not know. Certainly it is no credit to this country that we have to stand now, four years later, and say- especially with relation to a treaty with our brothers of the West Indies-that we have failed to comply with the terms of an engagement made with them.
Though I his has to be admitted, certain good results have accrued. Undoubtedly our trade has expanded. I do not say it is not capable of further expansion, but I must be pardoned if I express the fear that we cannot look for quite so much as the Minister of Finance expressed as his hope this afternoon. I am inclined to think that we are a lot nearer the maximum of our exports of the various articles which he recites in chief as Canadian products going to the West Indies, than he imagines. I think indeed that in some of them we have nearly a monopoly of those products which the people of the islands really consume. There are, besides white people, many blacks in those islands, and in some of the lines covered by the treaty they do not purchase the character of goods which we have for export. However, there will be room for some expansion, and I earnestly hope the terms of the treaty will prove such that expansion may take place.
