speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The picture painted by
the Minister of Finance as to the enhancement of our exports to the West Indies was, I think, somewhat rosy. In respect of flour I doubt if there is very much room for further expansion. The qualities of flour used there in so far as they are of the nature of the article



Canada-West Indies Agreement
that we produce at all are practically wholly bought from this country now. The same applies to lumber and many other things embraced in the treaty.
Coming to the other side of the trade feature, the imports from the West Indies, I hope there is more room for the optimism of the minister in that direction. As respects the great product of the larger dominions, bananas, it is true that notwithstanding the fact that under the old treaty the reduced tariff was open only to goods entering our ports, the great bulk, in fact the almost overwhelming proportion, came through the United States. I am not so sure that this treaty is going to effect so great a change. There are a great many factors entering into that situation, factors that will not be removed by the treaty at all and which will still militate against direct shipment. However, if the treaty does anything in that respect it will do a service to this country.
I am apprehensive of the loss of revenue from reductions made, especially on sugar. The minister did not give us any idea of what he expected there. We are reducing our tariff on sugar, we are not increasing it as respects other countries, and I think the minister will find that he or probably his successor, will have to do without something approaching a million a year. That is a large sum of money. Similar remarks would apply to other features of our imports. However, I believ i i the principle of giving to our Dominion, and especially giving to them in return for consideration given us, a preference over every country in the world in respect of articles consumed in Canada. That is what we have to give, that is what we ought to give, that is what we can give without militating against Canadian production; and for my part I would be slow to criticize treaties because of any vulnerable feature from that standpoint. If, however, the treaty, went to the impairment of Canadian production then it would take certainly a multitude of virtues to cover a sin in that respect.
As to the service features, I referred to them only briefly before six o'clock. I cannot understand why the minister is not able to give the House a rough estimate of what the new service features are to cost this country. In reply to a very direct question he said he could not do so for some time. Surely the government has not entered into a contract involving very large commitments, commitments which doubtless will run into millions, and yet is unable to give the House at least an estimate of what the aggregate is to be. I know there are very grave fears expressed in some quarters, where the opinion

should be the most intelligent, that these commitments are serious. Indeed, the commitments we made in respect of service under the treaty of 1920 evidently proved so onerous that this government could not comply with them. I am still not wholly clear as to why the compliance did not take place, but I am inclined to think that the government found itself unable to make compliance save by an extension of the service of the Canadian merchant marine.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They have made such a tremendous bogy of the merchant marine before the electors-in which possibly they were joined by the Saskatchewan colony, I do not know-but they have so condemned it and ridiculed it from end to end of Canada that notwithstanding the recommendations made to them for its extension in the West India service they did not do it, but rather put themselves in the position where they have to come to parliament and admit they have failed to comply with a solemn contract made on behalf of Canada. I think there was difficulty in living up to our engagements at the service in the treaty of 1920. How is it going to be easier to live up to far greater engagements? In this treaty without a doubt they are more serious. The minister knows they are more serious-especially as to one of these groups they are far more serious- and as a result this government will have to pay out very large sums of money indeed in subsidies, or they will have to extend the merchant marine service. I know they are in a quandary as to which they will do. I know they find difficulties both ways, difficulties they created very largely for themselves by spurious political propaganda. But anyway, though these commitments may be serious too, I am disposed to sympathetically view the whole situation as to this treaty. I believe it has very important significance from an empire standpoint. Hon. gentlemen have often ridiculed this idea. I do not mean those very close to me, but hon. gentlemen at other angles of this House have often ridiculed the idea that trade has anything to do with nationality, that trade relations necessarily involve political relations. I want just to suggest this thought to hon. members of this House; it is just because trade has a lot to do with nationality, it is just because trade relations are bound up with political relations, that this treaty comes before this parliament at this time. It is because of the importance of this treaty to national and political relations with the West India islands that it appeals most strongly and will appeal most strongly to hon. members of this House.

Canada-West Indies Agreement
I believe, indeed, the government would do themselves credit to admit that this factor of the situation had very much to do with the whole matter of the negotiation of the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that
from the Prime Minister. It is creditable to the government that it had so to do with the negotiation of the treaty; but I want to know why it is that the trade relations of the West Indies with the United States are inseparably and inexplicably involved with their political relations with that country, and the trade relations of Canada with the United States have nothing whatever to do with the political relations of Canada with the United States. I am glad that the light has come in, even though it had to come from the far off West Indies to reach the mind of the government in this regard.
So I say, reserving certain criticism which would be more appropriately addressed to the government in committee, and reserving the right of course to make suggestions with relation to it-and I have in mind one especially as respects the sugar refining industry of British Columbia-I am disposed to welcome the advent to this parliament of any effort to tie more closely our brothers of the West Indies to ourselves in any trade treaty.

This
is a very interesting subject to me, and has been very interesting since the close of the Great war. From November 11, 1918, when the Armistice was signed, I conceived the idea that Canada should have some territona! rights in a tropical or semi-tropical country, to produce the things that we need, so as to assist in repaying us for the great expense to which thig country was subjected in our efforts to win the world war. Coming to this House shortly afterwards I found that the champion of the development of West Indian trade was F. H. Keefer; I forget what portfolio he held. He had been down to the West Indies on a trip, and I approached him in order to get some information. 1 found that the ideas which Canadians generally had on this subject were absolutely wrong. On Armistice day I was called upon to make a speech in my county and in mv remarks I stated that Canada should have territorial rights in some tropical country A very well-informed man whom I met at lunch that day said, "What do we want of 15,000,000 niggers?" On coming here I went to the library and found that the population 14011-110i
of the West Indies was about one-third English, one-third French and one-third Spanisa, the total less than 3,000.000. Mr. Keefer was very much interested, and was pleased to _ get even one person to raise his voi'e in this House in favour of commercial union. I am a political unionist.
Mr. O'NEILL: What is the name of the minister?
- Mr. BALDWIN:	Frank H. Keefer, a
member of this House under the ministry of the Borden government. I obtained information which I had never received before I got information from Harry Crow, who had a long and extended acquaintance with the British West Indies. He was a political unionist and favoured a commercial union between Great Britain, the Crown colonies and the dominions of the West Indies. When we speak of the West Indies we must remember that there are innumerable islands, the Leeward, the Windward and a multitude of other islands, and their possibilities of production are tremendous.
I have been watching the great American republic to the south of us for many years, and I have observed that through their diplomacy and their methods of conducting affairs they have acquired great territories that will produce tropical and semi-tropical products. Here we have a country in Canada covering one-half of the North American continent, without one inch capable of producing tropical or semi-tropical products. It appears to me very desirable that we should obtain a footing in the West Indies. Mr. Crow spent a great deal of time and a fortune in advancing ideas of political union.
Mr. Macaulay of the Sun Life had made many trips to the British West Indies in connection with his great company, and he maintains that commercial union is very much needed. Whether a continuous agreement or any agreement that would be never ending were made, would be immaterial; but let us see how much we need their produce and how much they need ours. We require in this country all the products which they produce. It is within the realm of possibility that they will learn to produce rubber in British Guiana and British Honduras, and that they will produce cotton and everything in that line that we will require. What a splendid chance fr Canada in this line. The people of the West Indies, in the development of these islands, require the manufactured goods we produce in Canada, and they need the natural products of this country. Mr. Keefer was sent down there by the Borden government, and Sir George Foster has made many trips to that

Canada-West Indies Agreement
country investigating conditions. I dislike to suggest what'I might possibly think-that the opposition were not able to conclude trade relations or to negotiate favoured nation agreements, and they are simply not pleased that this government has about consummated what they worked for years and years to accomplish and failed.
My hon. friend is wrong.

Why am I wrong?
Pray tell me.
Did they not make some treaties with the West Indies?

Yes but those treaties
availed very -little indeed.
Our Maritime provinces are crying for Maritime rights. Now if we can get a market for the products of the east and the west of Canada by giving to the West Indies a market for their produce, will that not be beneficial to the Maritime provinces? In Halifax they have great storehouses where they -could store these products and a splendid trade could be built up.
I believe that Canada is going to make rapid progress; the population will in a few years be much greater than it is to-day. If we can get a market for our manufactured products, *our condensed milk and dairy products in the West Indies, it would be a great thing; our trade would grow and gro-w and it would make us independent of other countries. It would also furnish traffic for our railways and our steamships. There is nothing selfish about this. The provinces of British Columbia and Alberta will send their fruit out to the Pacific ocean and it will be shipped through the Panama canal to the West Indies. So that there is no part of Canada that will not be benefited; all the products of the different provinces will be shipped by rail and water. There is no reason therefore, why this agreement should not be consummated. As to the bugaboo that many features of this treaty are unfavourable to this country, when we think of those far distant lands of Australia and New Zealand away down on the rim of the world, why should we be afraid of their products that will take seven or eight -weeks to reach Canada, when the great markets of the world are much nearer to us than to them.
A great deal has been said about butter. A few weeks ago some members of the opposition, speaking in the House, were making it almost a point that the farmers of this country were going to be destroyed owing to importations of butter. Butter has been advancing in price, and I believe the poor people of this country must be eating their bread

dry at the present time because butter at the lowest price is costing forty-seven cents a pound and none can be procured for less. I do not think it would be a crime if the great, consuming public of Canada could get butter for a little while at a lower price, and surely our farmers are receiving a price with which they are quite satisfied.
Under this favoured-nation treaty that is being made with the British West Indies, our butter, cheese, condensed milk, flour and vast quantities of manufactured goods can be exported into those colonies under a preference that will give us almost a monopoly. Who for one moment could think that would not be a great advantage to Canada? On the contrary let me tell the House a few things that transpired during the late Conservative regime. We were importing $100,000,000 worth of fruits principally from the United Fruit Company, a great octopus company in the United States. At that particular time they were paying for the goods in the West Indies when the dollar was about equal to sixty cents, and they were re-selling them to Canada making from 12 to 20 per cent of a discount on the Canadian dollar In other words, for the $100,000,000 worth of fruit that was imported from the British West Indies this company was making a profit of over $50,000,000. If we look at the matter from any point of view it makes a Canadian look small.
I wish Canadians when going to a sunny clime would travel via Halifax and boat to the British West Indies although if they want to go by way of the United States, the trip will be a shorter one. But let them visit the British West Indies and learn of our brothers there. One important thing we can learn from them is that they speak better English than we do. I noticed last spring even as regards the coloured members of the delegation which came here from the British West Indies, their dialect was such that they spoke perfect English. There is no place on the American continent where they speak as good English as in the state of Virginia where the old colonial English are now kept intact and they send their sons and daughters back to England to be educated. It almost makes me ashamed to speak to those people. It would be a much shorter trip to visit the British West Indies than to go to California. We should learn from those people in the British West Indies and they could learn from us. We could consummate trade with them; we would have much better enjoyment for less money and we would come to a fuller realization of the greatness of the British Empire. Should political union come, which I am very much

Canada-West Indies Agreement
interested in, I do not know that they would send members to this House of Commons, but they might send members to the Senate. They could be represented in this parliament in some way, and I have no fear that a population of around three million could ever dominate this great country.
Notwithstanding all the drawbacks we may have had in the past few years, we are going to make great progress in Canada. The United States is being filled up; its lands are being held now at almost fabulous prices; they are dyking back the seas and making land costing over a thousand dollars an acre. They are constructing roads up the highest mountains and over the deserts, but they cannot continue in that way so that people will come to our great country, and develop our great resources in agriculture, forests, fisheries and perhaps the greatest wealth of all, our mines. The people of the British West Indies will be great consumers for our fisheries, and from every point of view there need be no parochial thought about this. As I have said the extreme western part of Canada produces beautiful apples, and I do not know but the time may come when they can raise figs, as I hope they will be able to do although at present they are importing them from California. But notwithstanding all that, in order to keep a healthy body we must eat green things; we need fruits that we cannot raise in Canada, but that can be produced by the cheap labour in the British West Indies and brought here by boat to nourish our bodies.
From every point of view there is not the least doubt that the consummation of this treaty will be of great benefit to Canada and of as great benefit to the people of the British West Indies. As it is dull to listen to a member talking extemporaneously on this matter after hearing the Minister of Finance-and after all others will follow me who will give exact figures-I will not make any further remarks with regard to this question which is very dear to my heart.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in accord with the principle of this resolution, and I should like to say a few words about it before it goes tc the committee. Everyone knows I stand first for Canadian interests, and I believe in giving as much work as we possibly can to our own people. I do not want any treaty that is going to reduce work in Canada. At the same time I am one of those who believe firmly that our British commonwealth of nations can be made self-sustaining. We know that we can produce within the commonwealth everything that we require either for
our comfort or for the safety of the empire. This was demonstrated beyond any question in the war when our supplies from foreign sources were cut off and we were obliged to produce more food and to make munitions and other necessary equipment for the safety of ourselves and of the British Isles. At that time the people of the British Empire enormously increased their production and proved to the world that they could produce everything that was required within the commonwealth. Why should we not take every step we can to make that condition permanent ''
The United States has attained its present great strength as a result of the pursuit of just such a policy: she trades within herself and her home market is the one that is of value to her. We in Canada have also a home market but we can at the same time create within the whole empire a home market on a larger scale, a British home market. I say therefore that it is the duty, as it would be to the advantage, of every part of this commonwealth of nations to adopt the principle of buying from sister nations what the people at home cannot produce for themselves. That, as I say, is the policy that has produced such excellent resuits in the United States and it is equally the policy that can make a success of the British commonwealth of nations. To bring this about we must trade with one another to as large an extent as possible and this treaty is to my mind a distinct step in that direction.
I was sorry indeed to hear the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) bringing party issues into the discussion to-night, for one of the things in regard to this treaty that pleases me most is the continuity of policy which has characterized one government after another in Canada,. This has been so for years, and I am firmly of the opinion that in regard to all questions of foreign policy, including relations between different parts of the empire, there should be a continuity of policy. None of these questions should be discussed from the party point of view. In the case of this treaty hon. gentlemen opposite have followed in our steps, just as we endeavoured to follow in the steps of those who went before us, in order to bring about favourable relations with the British Islands and the West Indies.
Years ago I was much interested in this question, having ior a considerable period at various times administered the Department of Trade and Commerce. While in that position I learned a good deal about this

Canada-West Indies Agreement
interesting problem. The products raised in the West Indies are complementary to those that we produce in this country, and are in no way competitive with them. It is true we buy a lot of these things from the United States, and that is one practice I should like to see put an end to. I earnestly hope therefore that this steamship service which is about to be arranged for will have the effect of increasing our imports of these commodities from the British West Indies rather than from the United States. We in Canada need a good deal of the products of the tropics, and it is only natural that we should buy them from British countries. The British West Indies, embracing such islands as Bermuda, as well as British Guiana on the mainland and British Honduras, are all friendly to us, and while we require the things they produce they on the other hand need the products that we raise in this northern zone. Now those islands are all contiguous to the United States. At any rate they are nearer to the United States than to us, and I for one hope that we shall do everything we possibly can to keep them British. We should do our share in that direction, and I consider that this treaty has that tendency.
As the United States is a very strong magnet to these islands, we must, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said, develop inter-imperial trade if we are to preserve our British sentiment, as no doubt we all desire to do. Several prominent men in Canada have for years taken a great interest in this question. I have had conversations with many of them at various times in London when the matter has been fully discussed. I may say that they welcome the treaty as a fulfilment of some of their wishes. While I am on this subject I may observe that we were all very pleased to see the delegates from the islands and from Demerara. Personally I found them men of ability and ol broad views who could understand our Canadian conditions and problems, and they showed themselves in every way friendly to us and our ideas. I very much hope that we shall see them frequently.
I am not very familiar with the details of this resolution, but we naturally expect that this government will have made some mistakes in the matter. It would be very extraordinary if they did not. At the same time, however, we trust that they have not injured any of our Canadian industries in arranging the details of the agreement. The items of the treaty will of course be discussed in committee, but I just want to refer in passing to the matter of the" steamship service. The Min-

ister of Finance (Mr. Robb) does not feel disposed to tell us how much the service is likely to cost, and I take it that he does not wish to disclose that in advance of receiving tenders for the service, but I am very much afraid that it will be a costly piece of business. All we can hope is that the traffic between this country and the West Indies will be so developed that the expense we shall incur may be justified. At any rate I want to say at this juncture that I am in favour of the principle of the treaty, for the reason that it will help to develop trade between the various nations and sections of the British commonwealth, and thus be another step in the direction of making that commonwealth self-sustaining.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had not intended taking part in the discussion but I feel that this is an occasion on which it should be made apparent to the country that happily, for once, both opposition and government seem to be in entire accord on a great principle which we ail have very much at heart, namely, the principle of developing as far as possible, by means of trade and in other ways, the relations that bind together the different parts of the British empire.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) said he was pleased that the government appeared to have received more light in the matter of treaty relations within the empire' than it had previously had. I am afraid my right hon. friend has forgotten his own speeches in the Maritime provinces made so recently as a few months ago. This treaty was negotiated last summer by members of the government who at that time met delegates from the British West Indies. The conference was held in Ottawa, and as a result a treaty was signed which was subsequently printed and distributed to the press in all parts of the Dominion. The government felt that it had not only rendered a definite service to Canadian trade, but also the kind of service to which hon. gentlemen opposite have alluded to-night, namely that of helping to bind more closely together, through the agency of trade, different parts of the British empire. What was our amazement when we discovered that my right hon. friend in the course of his speeches in the Maritime provinces was declaring that so far as he was aware there was no such thing as a treaty even negotiated! He nevertheless condemned the treaty very strongly. He shakes his head now, but he has forgotten what he then said.

Canada-West Indies Agreement

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, I have not forgotten a word. I know what I said at that time. I said no such thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will he tell us what he did say?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly. I said I had never seen a copy of the treaty, and that I would not take any position for or against it until I had seen it. Whatever criticism I might have of it, I would not give judgment upon it until I had seen the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All I can say. Mr. Speaker, is that after the profession my right hon. friend has just made about desiring to further trade within the empire, it is extraordinary that he should now have to confess to the House that he went into a political campaign and criticized the administration on a treaty designed for the very purpose of closer trade relations within the empire, a treaty which he also said that he had never even seen! I was going to remind him of the fact that the statements he made throughout the Maritime provinces when he was campaigning there in the fall were first of all, as I understood, condemnatory of the treaty. However, I will take his word for it now that what he then said was not condemnatory, but was simply that he had not seen a copy of the treaty. I know he made that statement because I had him presented with a copy of the treaty myself. We happened both to be in the vicinity of Sussex, New Brunswick, the day after my right hon. friend asserted that he had not seen the treaty and that it was non-existent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He did not say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I sent him a copy of the treaty with my compliments. That evening he undertook to discuss the treaty at a meeting in Sussex, and he then condemned it. I have reports of his speech and the impression it created throughout the Maritime provinces was that the treaty was a mistake, that the government had done something that was wrong, and that this was one thing more for which fault should be found with the administration. Well, I am quite prepared to forgive my right hon. friend. I am glad he has seen the light; but I do not want him to come and tell this House and the country that the government has seen the light, when he himself was in such total darkness as not even to have had any knowledge of the treaty itself, if not also of its terms.
My hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) has referred to the importance of
linking together the different parts of the empire in matters of trade. May I say, Sir, that that is something which this government has had at heart not only with respect to this treaty, but also with respect to another treaty which some of his friends have condemned rather strongly, namely, the treaty with the great dominion of Australia. That treaty was also negotiated by this administration with the same belief that it was desirable to seek to bring about a closer bond of union between different parts of the empire.
May I suggest to the right hon. gentleman that that is a very different matter, because that treaty in many cases takes away work from our own people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not quite follow my hon. friend's point of view. As I understood, he wants to develop closer relations within the empire by trade. Australia is at one side of the globe and our Dominion is at the other. It is a vast range over which competition is taking place, and it is an extraordinary thing if this Dominion within its own boundaries cannot hold its own in competition with Australia. However, supposing it were true, which I do not admit, that the treaty did take away a certain amount of work from our people as my hon. friend suggests, I ask him: would he not feel that what might be gained by further strengthening the empire in many other respects would be fully equal to so small a sacrifice of a material character? If he is really sincere in bis talk of empire unity and. solidarity, he must, if need be, be prepared to make some little material sacrifice for it. If he is not, I may tell him that the present administration is so prepared to do, and we have so viewed these questions.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, I hope that what has been done in this treaty by way of furthering, as we trust, closer relations between the British West Indies and Canada may be extended to include possibly another British dominion in this western hemisphere. In addition to the West Indies there is the island colony of Newfoundland, which is a near neighbour of this country. I think something might be made of the fact that we have in this western hemisphere what may well be known as a British North America, composed of Canada, Newfoundland and the islands of the Atlantic generally classed as the British West Indies. It should be the aim and purpose of all of us who have at heart the interests of our own Dominion and the larger interests of the British Empire to seek to develop to the fullest possible extent that

Canada-West Indies Agreement
British North America in relations of trade, in relations of commerce and communication and in relations to friendship. I believe this treaty will go far towards developing trade with the West Indies. I believe it will do more than that. I believe the contacts it will lead to between the peoples of the West Indies and the people of our Dominion will be mutually helpful in directions that possibly very few of us at this moment can foresee. Certainly the meeting of the delegates here created the impression to which the hon. member for Argenteuil has alluded, namely that they cordially welcomed the closer relationships that were likely to grow out of this treaty.
In addition to trade, there is developing between the British West Indies and Canada an important tourist traffic. The two countries are the complements of each other; one is in the temperate zone, the other in the tropical; and it is the natural thing that at particular seasons the people of the British West Indies should look to Canada as the part of the empire to which they would be glad to come, and that we should look with equal desire upon the British West Indies as a part of the empire which our citizens will find it easy to visit and become acquainted with. This treaty as it has been drafted has had in mind not merely the purposes of trade but also of travel, and part of the money which has to go for subsidy purposes will be spent in increasing the facilities for travel between the British West Indies and this country.
Once again, .Sir, may I say what a pleasure and satisfaction it is to discover that at least on one measure both sides of this House appear to be united',-a measure which has bearings that are much larger than those of mere nationality, bearings that concern vitally the interests of the great empire of which we are a part.

May I ask the Prime
Minister if the different items of this treaty will come under consideration in committee of the Whole? I have not been able to be in the House during all the discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I merely want to ask the Prime Minister a question. He referred to a number of other countries that were likely to be benefited by this treaty. Would he be good enough to give us the names of those different countries? I am sure the information would be appreciated by the House.
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
Mr. MACKENZIE KING. I think my hon. friend must have misunderstood my remarks. I said there were different countries that composed what I termed a British North America, including Newfoundland, the islands of the British West Indies and some other idands. and of course our Dominion. I was there referring to something that I hoped this treaty might lead to-a further development of trade in directions which are not included in it at the present moment, but which may come to be included later on.
I understood that the preferential clauses in this treaty would be extended to other countries outside of the British West Indies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is a treaty with the West Indies.

Mr. Speaker, in making a few remarks with regard to this treaty I do not wish it to be understood that I am strongly opposed to any treaties that will lead to the development of Canadian trade. The object of all Canadian governments should be to increase our trade as far as possible, always having in view the economic position of this country, the cost of such extension, and the operation of such treaties. This West India treaty I think has some defects. In the first place, it was negotiated by representatives of Canada who never had been closely identified with the West Indies, and who had very little knowledge of West India trade and West India conditions, and that was done notwithstanding the fact that representations were made to the Department of Trade and Commerce at the time suggesting that in the interests of Canada the committee that dealt with this matter should contain some representatives who had a knowledge of the West India trade. Not only that, but the department was asked to have a conference with merchants and others who had been brought up in that trade and had been familiar with it from boyhood, having carried it on and been in close touch with it in some cases for forty or fifty years. But even this suggestion was not accepted, and, as I said before, the gentlemen composing that committee were wholly without practical knowledge of the West India trade.
I think that the treaty is faulty in many respects. When this matter was first brought up in the House last year by the then member for Cumberland, he painted a very glowing picture of the trade possibilities with the West Indies, running into millions indeed, I believe, almost hundreds of millions, of dollars' worth

Canada-West Indies Agreement
of trade which he thought might be done between Canada and our West India neighbours. As a matter of fact Canada to-day is receiving from the West Indian islands about all of their products that they can supply to this country; I am speaking now altogether of the eastern group of the West Indies, or what is generally known as the Windward islands group. Those islands produce four articles in quantity:	sugar, molasses, lime juice and
cocoa.
An hon. MEMBER; What about rum?

They do not produce very much rum. There is some rum coming from Demerara, but I may tell you that it is of rather an inferior quality. The four articles I have mentioned are the chief articles produced in those islands.
Taking first, sugar, Canada is now receiving from the West Indies all the sugar she requires. If she required more, the present subsidized steamship service is quite capable of carrying more freight, because on an average voyage of the steamers of the Royal Mail Steamship Company the cargo carried averages only from 65 to 67 per cent of the total carrying capacity. So that if more sugar is required in Canada from the West Indies, the tonnage is there to carry it; but it is not required.
Molasses is in the same position as sugar. We get from the eastern group of the West Indies all the molasses that Canada needs, and no increased service is going to increase that trade.
So far as cocoa is concerned, a few years ago, when I was looking around to increase our trade with the West Indies and increase the freight cargoes for our boats, I remember interviewing Cowan's, a large cocoa concern in Toronto, and urging them to get more of the West India cocoa for use in theii manufactures, and the reply I got-and the same thing applies I believe to Moir's of Halifax, a very large chocolate manufacturing concern there-was that in order to obtain the best quality of chocolate they had to mix the cocoa beans they got from the West Indies with the products of other countries, otherwise they would not get the best results. So I doubt very much if there can be any increase in the importation of cocoa, and even though there was a possibility of that, the quantity used in this country is very small indeed compared with the capacity of the steamers that even now are running on that route.
I do not think it is worth while spending very much time over lime juice, for the consumption is very small in this country. It
is certainly small in Nova Scotia, even undei prohibition. So I do not look forward to any great increase in our imports from the West Indies.
With regard to exports, we are to-day supplying the West Indies with all the chief articles which they require. Of flour, for instance, the eastern group take
9 p.m. from Canada about 98 per cent of their total flour requirements. They also take from this country the greatest proportion of their imports of mill feeds, although they do not keep very many horses or any other animals down there, and therefore the sale of these articles is not very great; but what they do take of flour and mill feeds they get very largely from Canada. The lumber they require is supplied chiefly from our provinces, and there can be no increased business in that article. Furthermore, lumber is an article which is carried at a low rate of freight on sailing vessels; it is not and will not be transported by steamer. The few sample lots of Douglas fir that have been sent to the West Indies have been favourably received, but of course there is no possibility of shipping that article from Atlantic ports.
In connection with this treaty it must be borne in mind that Great Britain is in precisely the same position as Canada with regard to the preference, and the articles which Great Britain at the present time is sending to the West Indies will continue to go there, I take it, under the same conditions that they would go if shipped to Canada, and these articles are largely those imported by Canada herself from Great Britain. In view of what I said, and perhaps I have not gone as fully into the matter as I should have, I do not see the possibility of any very great increased trade-^nothing to warrant the expensive steamers and the frequent sailings it is proposed to put on.
Cold storage is provided for in the treaty. There is not very much involved in that provision. I think the only islands that would make use of cold storage would be the larger ones, Barbados and Trinidad, and then Georgetown, Demerara, on the mainland. These islands and the mainland are farming countries. They have what they call their "penns"-in other words, farms-and they produce a great many of the products that might go out in cold storage. But on the return trip, I do not know what would be placed in cold storage, because the Windward islands and the mainland-the mainland especially-produce nothing but sugar and molasses. The islands are not adapted for the growing of fruit, and therefore there would be no fruit to fill that cold storage capacity. Even if there were

Canada-West Indies Agreement
cetera. Our manufactured goods come very largely from the United Kingdom, and the only article, as it appears to me, that we could encourage in trade with Canada by an increased preference, is the item of salted meats, which could be turned over to Canada, and would probably go over quicker if you got an increased preference. That is as far as I can see as far as Barbados is concerned.
What he says applies not only to Barbados but to all the islands of the West Indies and to Bermuda.
I do not know that I desire to say anything more at the present time in regard to this matter. As I said when I rose, I am not opposing any treaty or trade arrangements with any country from which treaty we shall derive a benefit, but I am strongly opposed to coupling up our steamship services with trade treaties. We have had experience enough, as I said before, with regard to the operation of steamers by government, and if this contract is taken on by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine the cost to this country will be a very serious matter.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended making a few general observations but they have been already referred to by some lion, members who have spoken, and I am going to coniine my remarks to some of the criticisms of the treaty made by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black). As one of his associates in framing this treaty, first of all I should like to pay tribute to the excellent work of the hon. member for Cumberland in the Iasi parliament who inspired the negotiations that took place between Canada and the sister colonies in the south. We have just heard it said that we cannot develop a business in fruit with the West Indies. That was the very thing that inspired Mr. Logan when he saw Canada importing practically 2,500,000 bunches of bananas, with only 700,000 bunches coming directly from the West Indies, the balance all coming through the United States. Fruit was one of the items in which he was most interested when he made his trip to the West Indies.
I should like to pay a tribute to the delegation which came here. W e found on meeting those gentlemen that they knew a good deal more about Canada than the Canadian delegates knew about the West Indies. For that reason I appreciate the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he says it is to be hoped that a better steamship service will induce many of us to travel to the 'West Indies for the winter instead of to Florida or California, and leam a little more about our sister dominions or sister 
colonies. If the steamboat service is good enough to induce Canadians to know the West India islands, I think it has in that respect alone served a very useful purpose.
I am rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax when he infers that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and the government did not know anything about what this service was to cost. It is quite true that you would not expect the Minister of Finance who intends to ask for tenders for this service to reveal to the agent of the West India Steam Packet Company who has just spoken, what he expects to pay them. The hon. member for Halifax is in the shipping business; his company has had contracts with governments of the past for this service. He knows that when his company got S131 ,400 per annum by way of subsidy we were doing only a very limited business with the West Indies, a business of imports of about $801,000 and of exports of $1,500,000 whereas the trade has grown to $14,000,000 of imports and $10,000,000 of exports. Any one who has seen the trade with the West Indies develop knows that we have built up in the last few years in one item alone, that of condensed milk, a business amounting to three-quarters of a million dollars. We have also built up a business in cheese, butter, cement and flour, the latter probably being the largest, but the fact remains that in many commodities, even our own fruits which they do not grow, such as apples, we have built up a substantial trade. The hon. member for Halifax and some business men in that city are objecting very strenuously to the cost of the service. As an Ontario business man I am prepared to pay my share of the cost of this service as a contribution to imperial unity, and I cannot see why a Halifax merchant who is going to receive a great deal more benefit than probably any Ontario man, should object if the rest of Canada including members like the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), the Prime Minister of Canada and others speak of the necessity of imperial trade and the desire if possible to further that trade.
I remember reading in the Toronto Saturday Night, a journal which is not noted for complimenting this government, shortly after the treaty was published, an editorial which said that critics of the King government would have a very difficult time to find fault with the West India treaty which had just been negotiated. I was thinking of that article to-night when I observed the laboured efforts of hon. gentlemen opposite to bring forward

Canada-West Indies Agreement
something against the treaty. I believe that when we go into committee and the agreement is considered item by item it will be very difficult indeed for hon. members to find very many flaws in it.

Can the hon. member
tell us the number of bunches of bananas imported into Canada from the West Indies?
About 700,000 direct.
That is not my question. Of the total number imported into Canada how many are grown in the West Indies?

That is not the point I
was making. What I am pointing out is that we import a total Of 2,500,000 bunches of bananas from the United States and elsewhere and that a very large proportion of them could be bought direct from the West Indies. Indeed, the delegates from Jamaica declare that they are able to take care of the Canadian banana trade if they have the proper steamship service. Given that they are prepared to develop a fruit trade with Canada which would meet all our requirements.
I prefer to discuss the subject further when the agreement is under consideration in committee, but at the moment I may be allowed this observation: the government was actuated by a desire to promote imperial trade, and I believe that the people are prepared to make a substantial contribution to that end. In this regard I would refer to the criticism which 'has been levelled at the Australian treaty, which is a trade agreement of exactly the same nature as this. That criticism has been eminently unfair. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the Australian treaty will make it possible for ten million or twelve million pounds of butter to be imported into Canada, but they forget their own argument that the treaty was designed to benefit certain manufacturers. My hon. friends opposite have always contended on the hustings that in building up industry in the country you create a greater consumption for the farm products of the Canadian agriculturist, but critics of the treaty never say a word to the effect that the improvement in Canadian industry might well take care of all the additional buttei that could come from Australia. I do not see how hon. gentlemen can possibly criticize the Australian treaty on that score. In a country that produces 275,000,000 pounds of butter, roughly speaking, and exports 30,000,000 pounds, the home market cannot possibly be greatly affected by an importation of five, six, seven or eight million pounds of butter, especially in view of the fact that its industry
is benefited to such an extent as to consume very largely the excess imports.
The business men throughout Canada do not view with any degree of credit the opposition adverse criticisms of trade treaties that make business for the manufacturers of the country. I would point out to my Conservative friends opposite that their friends in industry -were anxious to see the Australian treaty put into effect, as I was myself, and we all looked forward to having a greater market among the dominions for the manufactured products of Canada. We hope that we shall be able to supply Australia and the West Indies with practically all their manufactured imports, thus taking away that business from the United States. If the treaties with Australia and the British West Indies which have been entered into by this government do not develop a greater manufacturing connection between those countries and Canada, I shall be very much surprised, for all the indications to-day are that they will. This treaty with the West Indies was made in good faith but the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black) thinks that those who are interested in its negotiation do not know very much about business in the West Indies. I suppose that in order to know anything about West Indian or international business for that matter, one must live in Halifax. Let me tell the hon. member, however, that the Canadian members of the conference with the records of the Department of Trade and Commerce before them, and the advice of the various delegates from -the West Indies, who surely know their own business, did carefully study the possibilities of trade so that they were able to submit for the consideration of parliament an agreement -based on a -thorough investigation and a complete inquiry into all the details. Our hope is that the agreement will lead to further trade relations with the islands of the West Indies, to the advantage not only of the contracting parties, but of the empire as a whole.
Mr. ROBERT K. SMITH (Cumberland): It is not my purpose to discuss this subject at any length; I shall -be very brief. I want to say however, at the very outset, that during the last election we of the Maritime provinces were told that we must look overseas for -our markets, and I believe I am correct in attributing that statement to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The same thing was said by other Liberals in the Maritime provinces during the campaign. Now, if this treaty is brought forward as a means of solving the difficulties of the Maritime provinces I must say that we in that

Canada-West Indies Agreement
part of the country seriously object to it on that ground as the only remedy which the government intends to apply to the evils that have existed since confederation and are now so oppressive in those provinces. I hope it will be clearly understood by every member of this House that, whether this treaty is ratified or not, it is not intended as a means of solving our many problems 'by providing markets beyond the seas.
Another statement was made on the floor of this House to-night by the Prime Minister, a statement which was not only a gross exaggeration but a 'base misrepresentation of the attitude of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) towards the treaty with the West Indies as stated by him during the last election campaign. I understood the Prime Minister to say that the leader of the opposition in the campaign in the Maritime provinces condemned the West Indies treaty. I wish to say, speaking from firsthand knowledge, that this was not the case.
-Mr. MACKENZIE KING: Will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt him? He says that I have misrepresented the leader of -the opposition in this regard. I have in my hand at the moment a despatch that appeared in the Montreal Gazette and which I think I may quote as being -fair to my right hon. friend. It reads:
Meighen Warns Maritimes On New Trade Pact After Cursory Perusal He Says It Will Cost Millions (By Canadian Press)
Sussex, N.B., September 22.-Having obtained a copy of the West Indies treaty from the Prime Minister's train which passed through here early this afternoon, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Conservative leader, subsequently warned the people of the Maritime provinces not to be too optimistic about the new trade pact. "I have just made a cursory perusal of the treaty," Mr. Meighen told a large audience in the rink here, "and all I have to say is 'don't get too optimistic about it.' The features of most prominence in it are the bills. It will cost millions."
That is the extent to which the right h-on. gentleman dwelt upon the advantages of the treaty from an imperial point of view.

It makes no difference what the Montreal Gazette or any other newspaper says, although I do not object to what the Prime Minister has just read in this connection inasmuch as there is nothing in the quotation to show that the leader of the opposition condemned the treaty. But I can give the Prime Minister some firsthand information on the matter. I was present at a meeting in the town of Amherst at which the leader of the opposition had spoken, and after he had taken his seat someone in the galleries asked; "What about the West Indies treaty?" He had finished his speech at

that time, but he got up and said in effect: I am not in a position to take any definite stand on the West Indies treaty until I have studied it from begining to end; I am not in a position to condemn it, nor will I condemn it now, but I have heard from various sources that it will be an expensive experiment. I think that is pretty nearly quoting exactly what the right hon. leader of the opposition said in this regard. If that is "condemning" the West. Indies treaty, then I do not understand my leader's language as does the right hon. Prime Minister.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but it was not published in the press of the Maritime provinces during the campaign that the leader of the opposition was condemning the treaty. The trade agreement was signed, I believe, in July; the election followed very closely in October, so that the people had not very much time to study and investigate it. I was up against the problem in my own county of Cumberland, where Mr. Logan my opponent, who had been largely instrumental in bringing about this agreement, brought it before the electors. And what was our answer? That we were not in a position to condemn the treaty; t-hat we had not bad an opportunity of studying it; that it would have to come before both houses of parliament for ratification; and that upon the floors of parliament it would be ascertained whether it was of virtue or not. That is the position we took in Cumberland county, and I believe a similar position was taken in every other county in the Maritime provinces.
As has been mentioned by other members who have preceded me in this connection, the main objection to the treaty has been the cost o-f the steamship service. We would fall short in our duty as Canadians and as partners in the imperial federation if we condemned a trade treaty with another portion oif the empire which was to -be of some benefit to us. We consider that this treaty will be of some benefit to us. But taking the benefits on the one hand and the expenditures on the other, it should be our duty to endeavour to find out whether they balance or not. That was our stand then, it is our stand now. We all desire imperial trade. There can be no difference of opinion on that ground, -and there will not be, providing the benefits and expenditures at least equalize each other; but there will be a very serious opposition if they do not. When we go into committee and discuss the details of this agreement clause by clause, I hope to become thoroughly conversant with it. On the principle of beneficial

Canada-West Indies Agreement
trade arrangements, as I said before, there is no difference of opinion. The only question is whether for the money expended we are going to secure anything like commensurate results.
In closing. Mr. Speaker, let me repeat what I stated in my opening remarks, tihat we in the Maritime provinces will not feel that by the passing of this treaty, if it does pass, our problems have been solved by any means.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from the Maritime provinces, where this is looked upon as a very important treaty, I crave the indulgence of the House while I make a few observations upon it. In the first place, as has been already said, the treaty provides for an exchange of products between the two countries. The province of Prince Edward Island is altogether agricultural, and our products have to find an outlet somewhere; that is our difficulty at the present time. Our friends opposite have said in the course of various debates in this House that it was a good thing for the Maritime provinces that the reciprocity pact was defeated. Well, I may say that they will have a great deal of difficulty in making a Maritime audience believe their statement, and they will have still greater difficulty in convincing a Prince Edward Island audience, because as we cannot find a market for our farm products in the other portions of the Dominion beyond what we are able to dispose of in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, we are forced to send our surplus into the United States against an almost prohibitive duty.
Now, I am glad to see our friends of the opposition approving of this treaty to a certain extent. As fair-minded men from all parts of Canada, I think we ought to view the treaty as broadly as possible, and carefully look into its provisions in committee to see that no mistakes are made; but let us endeavour, if possible, to secure the advantages which this treaty will undoubtedly give us, because, as my good friend from Cumberland (Mr. Smith) has said, we have Maritime rights to be considered, and our friends of the opposition have been advocating Maritime rights. I should like hon. members to know that here, I am confident, is one of the things that is going to help us overcome some of our Maritime difficulties. If there is a Maritime right to be brought up in the House this session that is more important than this treaty, I should like hon. gentlemen in whatever quarter of the House they may sit to tell us what it is.
Various views have been expressed regarding the cost of the boats that will have to be subsidized, and on other questions. I notice that
under this agreement we are for the first time to get a substantial subsidy from the West India islands to help the steamship service that the Canadian government has been subsidizing. That subsidy amounts to $142,000 per year, according to the treaty. Hitherto Bermuda has never contributed anything towards the cost of this steamship service, but they did contribute some $121,000 annually to American steamships to encourage them to trade with the British West Indies. This departure alone is a very important feature. Therefore, I repeat, we should consider this treaty in a broadminded way. I have in my hand a clipping from the Montreal Gazette in which reference is made to Mr. T. B. Macaulay, of Montreal, as one of the gentlemen who was largely instrumental in the treaty negotiations. The Gazette also contains cables from the British West Indies to that gentleman suggesting that if possible the treaty should be put through in its entirety. One of these cables from the Jamaica Imperial Association reads as follows:
We strongly urge Canada-West Indies Trade Treaty should pass in entirety as any (modification would amount to new proposal and would necessitate entirf agreement being reconsidered by colonial legislatures which means delay and uncertainty.
I have here a number of telegrams along the same line from the different legislatures, which I shall not take time to read. As I have said, I think we should take up this treaty item by item and endeavour to put it through as nearly as possible in the form that was agreed upon by the delegates from the West Indies when they were here.
What are some of the benefits that will accrue to the Maritime provinces from this treaty? In the little province of Prince Edward Island alone we raised last year over $7,000,000 worth of potatoes, the bulk of them for export. Our friends of the opposition have taken exception to a statement in the Speech from the Throne and have said that the government was endeavouring to take to itself the credit that belonged to Providence for the splendid crops we had throughout Canada last year. That is all right, but I would like to point out to them that in our little province alone we could triple in one year our production of potatoes with the help of a kind Providence, if only we could find an outlet for that increased production. Instead of growing only $7,000,000 worth of potatoes for export, within two or three years we could grow $25,000,000 worth, if we could only find an outlet for that production. We hope that this agreement will give us an outlet for some of our surplus products,

Ca?iada-West Indies Agreement
especially seed potatoes. This year, instead of the people of Prince Edward Island being encouraged to increase their acreage and produce more potatoes, they are being advised by our papers at the present time not to overproduce, because if they do it is said they will have no outlet for their products and the result will be a slump in price, and the growers will lose money, instead of making a small profit. That is the campaign that is being carried on by our papers at the present time, all because of our restricted market. Now that is a very serious state of affairs, and if this agreement will do anything to encourage even that one industry alone, I think it should receive the support of every member of this House.
Take dairy products, for instance. Last year we manufactured over SI,150,000 worth of butter, and cheese. In those two articles also we have a very large surplus for which we must find an outlet, and although we have a good trade with Great Britain, especially in cheese and butter, there is a possibility of obtaining a better price in the West India market for part of our product, and the same as to fish and other products.
Mr. Hodgson, of the firm of Hodgson Brothers, Montreal, is quoted as follows in the Montreal Star of July 9, 1925, regarding this trade agreement:
Local exporters, particularly of dairy products, are elated at the terms detailed in the text of the new trade agreement between Canada and the West Indies. In this connection. A. J. Hodgson, president of the Montreal Butter and Cheese Export Association, made the following statement: "The new agreement should prove a great benefit to the country at large, and should promote an increase in the dairy business everywhere in Canada."
It is contended by our friends of the opposition that the Australian treaty may injure our dairy industry in Canada, but when the treaty has been tested I do not think that contention will be borne out by the facts. Taking the treaties as a whole that have been negotiated by tlhis government, I think our dairy industry will not suffer, but rather that the situation will be greatly improved.
My good friend from Cumberland (Mr. Smith), who preceded me, has referred to the fact that Mr. Logan was largely interested in putting this treaty through. We all know the splendid efforts that Mr. Logan made on behalf of this trade agreement, and we can read in Hansard the very elaborate details that he gave in respect to every 10 p.m. line of trade that is dealt with in the agreement that is now before the House. He showed the tremendous possibilities of increased trade between the

two countries, especially in the products we raise in the Maritime provinces. I noticed a very strange thing in the last campaign in the Maritime provinces, and that was that this agreement was not praised at all by our friends opposing us, but rather they threw cold water upon it, and declared it was something about which we should be very, very careful and not be too optimistic over. I have a quotation here from The Ottawa Journal in which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is quoted as saying:
There is not one dollar in the West India Trade agreement for the people of the Maritime provinces.
I hope he has not been misquoted again, but if he has, it is only one more of numerous instances of which we have heard this year. One of the strange features of the last cam-paijpL in the Maritime provinces was that the three premiers of the Maritime provinces went to the town of my good friend from Cumberland, the town of Amherst, in order to defeat Mr. Hance Logan, the gentleman who was primarily instrumental in having this trade agreement -brought before parliament. Those three gentlemen combined their efforts to defeat Mr. Logan. I am not saying that this trade agreement was the only matter that was discussed, but I do say that our friends should be consistent; but what do we find? Immediately after the Dominion election the government of Prince Edward Island took upon itself to send a trade commissioner of their own to the British West Indies, clothed with all the power the local government could give him, to negotiate for trade with these islands. Our friends should be -consistent, and instead of endeavouring to defeat the gentleman who was * instrumental in bringing this agreement into its present form, they and the Maritime provinces would have done very well to give Mr. Logan the credit he deserves. I admit, of course, that the constituency of Cumberland is at present represented in this House by a very capable gentleman, who will no doubt do his very best for his constituency and the Maritime provinces generally, but I did wish to pay this tribute to Mr. Hance Logan, because he put more effort into this trade agreement than any other man in this chamber or any other man in the Maritime provinces during the four years we were here in the last parliament. I do not think it is necessary for me to say anything further in regard to the treaty, except that I believe it will be of immense benefit to us in the province of Prince Edward Island, because the British West Indies can use a certain amount of every product we have to export. We wish this treaty to be given a fair trial, and if that is done, and we

Canada-West Indies Agreement
endeavour to develop our trade with the West Indies, I believe this agreement will redound to the benefit not only of our province but of the Dominion as a whole.

I desire to make a few brief observations in regard to this trade agreement. In the first place I was much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) who spoke just a few moments ago. I am sorry he is not now in his seat, because I wanted to congratulate him upon the statement he made which I take to be a prelude to his introduction to this House as a possible Minister of Trade and Commerce in this dying government. Personally I have a very high opinion of the ability of the hon. member for North Bruce. He is a charming gentleman of considerable intellectual powers, a thorough protectionist in principle and in practice. I should like to say this for the benefit of our friends from Saskatchewan, that they will find him, as we have found him, very sound on the principles of protection especially with reference to the furniture business.
A future minister.

A would-be future minister.
Now, I want to approach this treaty, and the general principles underlying it, with the utmost consideration. That was the viewpoint of my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) from the very inception of the negotiations which resulted in this agreement in the month of July last. I remember very well when the delegates from the British West Indies assembled in this city in the month of June last. I remember very well a public statement made by my right hon. leader, in or near the city of Ottawa, in the presence of these delegates and I believe in the presence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, when he told them publicly that his attitude towards this treaty would be one of the utmost sympathy, not so much because he considered that any great material advantage would result to this country, but be-uon-m
cause of the fact that it would tend to foster so-called inter-imperial trade. For that reason I have endeavoured myself to view the negotiations, and the treaty itself, with the utmost sympathy.
Speaking particularly from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces-and naturally we drift more or less into local considerations,- I do not look for any very great increase of trade as a result of this treaty. It must be borne in mind that the treaty is with the British West Indies, and not with the West Indies alone. The big thing from the standpoint of the Alaritime provinces, if we could get it, would be a trade treaty with Cuba, which has a big purchasing power and contains a big consuming population. Just in that connection let me say that while this treaty was negotiated and the agreement signed in the month of July last, the treaty itself has never been brought before parliament until this stage of the present session. Nevertheless, on the part of members then supporting the government, from the Prime Minister himself down-not excluding my good friend Mr. Logan, an enthusiast in this matter, and to whom I believe a meed of praise is due for his energy in bringing this matter before the public mind of Canada and before parliament-there was the obvious desire to make political kudos out of this matter. Before the treaty had ever been submitted to parliament we were told down in the Alaritime provinces that we were dependent upon export trade. The Prime Minister told the people of Amherst, if I recollect aright, that our whole salvation depended upon export trade. Well, I believe in export trade for the Maritime provinces, but I question very much the ability of that portion of Canada to grow and prosper on export trade merely to the British West Indies, with a consuming public whose purchasing power, I suppose, is the lowest of almost any people on the civilized globe except that of the wilds of Africa or the west coast of that continent. Take butter alone. It is said that we would develop a large increase in the products of the dairy industry. Let my hon. friends read the report of the government's own trade commissioner, and they will note that outside of an exclusive and very limited circle the only butter which is in demand is cooking butter, and I doubt if any business house in Canada will make any very great efforts to follow up that class of business.
Speaking in connection with the potato growing industry, which has been referred to by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean), let me say that we supply the island



Canada-West Indies Agreement
of Bermuda with seed potatoes. There they grow their own potatoes, and they grow them not only for local consumption but for export. The earliest potatoes that appear on the New York market are Bermuda potatoes. Bermuda is exporting .them to that market to-day, and the only .potatoes imported into the island are seed potatoes. The people there do not grow seed potatoes themselves; they have to renew their seed every year, and the same is true of other West India islands. To-day we supply practically one hundred per cent of their demands. I should like to point out this though-that gentlemen supporting the government in the last campaign told the people in the Maritime provinces, the .people of New Brunswick-and I understood from an hon. member of this House that candidates representing the government told the people of Prince Edward Island-that as a result of this treaty Canada would have a preference in the Cuban market; they failed to lay emphasis on the fact that this was an agreement purely with a very limited population in the British West Indies as against the population of the whole of the West Indies, which has a very large buying power. As I said before, the big thing from the standpoint of the West Indies for the Maritime provinces would be a trade treaty with Cuba, but under present political conditions in that country that is impossible; that trade seems to have been coralled by our friends to the south.
But I do view with a very considerable degree of sympathy the making of a trade agreement such as this. I intend to vote for the .treaty unless it is made apparent that the cost in dollars and cents to the Canadian treasury is too great.	On that point we
have not been vouchsafed a tittle of information by the Minister of Finance to-night; he takes refuge behind the fact that he is now calling for tenders for the West India service. While that temporarily may be a good reason, I should like to say here that before the minister asks this House to ratify this treaty, before the imprimatur of our two houses of parliament is put upon this agreement, he should tell what we shall have to pay in dollars and cents. There is no question that the loss of revenue from sugar, and one or two other items, will represent a bill of a million dollars per annum. As was stated by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr Black) I doubt very much whether the Canadian consumer of sugar will benefit to the extent of a farthing from that reduction in duty. Nevertheless it may be that we should be willing to assume the responsibility of 
that loss of revenue and the shifting of the burden of taxation to something else in order to foster trade treaties of this character.
There is a further objection to this treaty, and that is that it is linking up with what is purely a trade arrangement, a proposition for a steamship service. I do not want to enter into any detail.
