I quite agree that in the trade treaty that already exists there was an undertaking to carry on steamship communication. But the service that is now agreed upon, as compared with that which has previously been carried out, is so great and so extensive that I doubt very much whether the government will be able, without the expenditure of several million dollars per annum, to induce any steamship company to carry on these operations, and I very much fear that as a result of the commitment of the government in this connection we shall be in the steamship business, operating between Canada and the British West Indies, before this matter is concluded. I warn the government that they ought not to do that. If there has been no complaint on the part of the British West Indies-and we have heard of none; at least the Finance minister has not taken us into his confidence to that extent-as to the character of the sendee in the previous year, and if the cost of the new proposed service is as large as some of us anticipate, I think there ought to be a modification of this particular part of the agreement.
I should not like to see the government and the country too optimistic about the benefits that may accrue to us from the West Indies trade agreement, especially those of us in the Maritime provinces. There are about three things we can export from New Brunswick to the West Indies: lumber, certain agricultural products, and possibly certain dairy products. Lumber now goes along well established routes by sailing schooners, so that it is not affected, and the treaty will be of no benefit in that respect. The amount of lumber that will be shipped to the British West Indies as a result of the agreement will never have any appreciable effect upon the lumber trade.
With respect to potatoes, we have the trade now in the Maritime provinces, and this treaty will be of no particular benefit to us. I venture the assertion that it will not increase the production of potatoes by 1,000 bushels per annum.
I should like to reserve whatever other remarks I desire to make in respect to this

Canada-West Indies Agreement
matter until we get into committee, with this statement, that the government should not have attempted during the last election to take to itself the kudos for entering into a trade agreement which, from the statements of its very sponsors, was supposed to have been kept out of the sphere of party politics, and for that the government and the Prime Minister himself are to be condemned.
Does the hon. member not know that great quantities of fish are shipped from St. John, New Brunswick to the West Indies?

I understand that that business is carried on through New York. If the hon. gentleman will consult the records of the Department of Trade and Commerce he will see that the people who import fish in the British West Indies buy only the meanest kind of fish. They buy dried hake, a kind of fish that neither my hon. friend nor any other self-respecting man would eat.

I am just as anxious as any other member of this House to develop trade within the British Empire, but I certainly do not wish to see that trade develop at the expense of industries in our own Dominion. I call attention of hon. members to the fact that this treaty will vitally affect one very important industry in my riding. Farmers living in western Ontario have a sugar beet industry of tremendous importance. Tens of thousands of acres of sugar beets are grown in that part of the province, valued at millions of dollars, and the profits to a considerable extent go back into the pockets of the farmers. It is a basic industry in that part of the country. In two sugar refineries alone, in Wallaceburg and in Chatham, at least $5,000,000 have been invested. In the town of Petrolia, where I live, we made an attempt a few years ago to build a sugar refinery. We are in the heart of the sugar beet industry, and that industry was being developed to an enormous extent prior to the action taken by this government in 1923. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that this government then reduced the duty on sugar one-half cent per pound. The very day after the duty was lowered the refineries in Walliaceburg and Chatham reduced the price of sugar beets to the farmers of that whole countryside fifty cents per ton. That might not have amounted to very much when sugar beets were selling at $8 or $10 a ton, but at the present prices of $5 or $6 a ton you can appreciate the fact that fifty 14011-1111
cents a ton is a very important consideration to the farmers of that country.
We had an organization of sugar beet growers in that district with over 4,000 members. Just about that time these men conceived the idea that the proper way for them to develop the industry was to build a sugar refinery in Petrolia. To that end they gathered together over $300,000, and they have already spent that amount on the sugar refinery, believing that they were going to receive fair consideration 'from this government. But the duty on refined sugar having been reduced by one-half cent per pound, what was the outcolme? Hon. gentlemen must recognize the fact that you cannot build a sugar refinery without spending nearly a million dollars. These men were carrying on a campaign for funds to develop the sugar refinery, but when the price of sugar beets was reduced it made it impossible for them to obtain capital and all their efforts went for nothing. The result is that buildings stand on those grounds to-day with the rafters up and without roofs-a monument to the folly of this government and the way they have conducted the affairs of this country.

friend talking such nonsense, when we have before us applications from the sugar beet people of Alberta to let in more men for the additional labour required in that province for the sugar beet business?

who live in the sugar beet area appreciate to the full that the time has come when our industry should receive some consideration at the hands of this government. I honestly hope that when we come to deal with the clauses of this treaty, every consideration will be given to the industry to which I have called attention to-night. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this time to deal at any length with the commercial phases of this question. That I think has been better dealt with by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) and some others who are better acquainted with that phase of the situation, than I am. The minister has referred to the character of the steamer service supplied the West Indies by Canada under the recent treaty and' he has stated that that service has not been satisfactory. That statement is well within the mark. The service was certainly not satisfactory to the people of the West Indies nor to the people who took advantage of it and travelled by it. That service was operating at one time with four and later three discarded boats of the Royal Mail service boats, which had formerly been employed in the South American trade and were out of date, foul smelling and lacking in accommodation. The proposal now, as I understand it, is that we should embark upon three different services at a cost for new vessels of probably between five and six million dollars. The senior member for Halifax has referred to the loss that is likely to ensue from the operation of these vessels and his

Canada-West Indies Agreement
estimate in that connection, is, I think, pretty close to the mark.
I wish particularly to call the attention of the House to the proposal to put on freight vessels to compete with private enterprises in the Maritime provinces and elsewhere. We have had quite enough of that in the last few years without embarking on any more of that particular kind of business. It is not fair that the government of this country should compete with private enterprise in matters of that kind. We have to-day a number of merchant marine vessels tied up in the port of Halifax and elsewhere eating their heads off, and if they could' be sold at even the prices obtained for boats that have been disposed of during the past two years, it would be good business for us to get rid of them.
One phase of the question seems to have some possibilities of merit. I refer to boats which, if of the character I have in mind, would capture the winter tourist trade of this country now running into enormous figures, and which trade is benefiting our friends of the [DOT] United States, especially California and Florida. Thousands and tens of thousands of Canadians are every winter travelling to those two states and spending anywhere from $30,000,000 to $100,000,000 annually in a foreign country. If we want to aid our compatriots of British origin in the West Indies, we should turn that trade their way instead of to California and Florida. I believe we could' do it to the advantage not only of the West Indies but of Canada as well. I would suggest putting on a fast service of 12 or 14-knot boats making weekly trips from the ports of St. John and Halifax alternately to the West Indies. Also run from Winnipeg weekly a special West Indies winter tourist train. That train could leave Winnipeg on Friday, running through Toronto and Montreal, get into Halifax or St. John on Sunday, and connect with those boats. This fast tourist train could thus collect tourists from Winnipeg and all the way down east to Halifax, destined for various West India islands, to the mutual advantage of Canada and that portion of the empire, for it would be a means of consolidating at least these two sections of the British commonwealth. The people of the British West Indies are just as British as we are. and I know of no better method than that I have just suggested of promoting good relations and a wider common understanding between us.
That brings me to another consideration. I have on a previous occasion spoken of Maritime rights, and while I will not dwell upon the subject to-night, I want to drop
a hint. It is sometimes said that if thf Maritime provinces letft the confederation they could do nothing by themselves. Well, perhaps they could not, and perhaps they could. I would remind the House, that the population of the three Maritime provinces combined totals about a million, and in any quarrel that might arise as a result of any dislocation in conditions in that part of the country, as they have existed since the first days of confederation, the three provinces would act together. I would ask hon. members this question: how has Newfoundland got along? That island has not been a part of the Canadian confederation, but is it not prosperous? Are the people of Newfoundland bankrupt? Have they made no progress? I will never admit for a moment that the people of the Maritime provinces could not get along alone and without assistance, but in conjunction with the island of Newfoundland could not the Maritimes make a treaty with the West Indies or with the United States, if to their advantage? At least, we would get along as well as we have during the last twenty years. I am not a secessionist and I hope I shall never have reason to be one; but whether I am one or not will depend altogether on t'he nature of the treatment accorded my part of the country by the other members of the confederation in the immediate future.

We are certainly living in a wonderful age, an age of conversion. We hear gentlemen getting up and telling us that they are absolutely opposed to the government going into business in competition with private interests and more particularly in the steamship enterprise. Yet when they were in power themselves they were so anxious to get into that business that they expended $75,000,000 in steamships, paying as high as $190 per ton at a time when the British government was offering for sale its own vessels at a price in the neighbourhood of $45. Let hon. gentlemen consider what their friends did when they were in office, and let them offer some justification for that conduct.
Not only are we living in an age of conversion, we are living in an age of discovery. It may be surprising to you, Mr. Speaker, as it is no doubt interesting to the young members in this section of the House, to know that we have discovered in this parliament so many new-found champions of the interests of the farmers. One of those champions has just taken his seat in the person of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong).

Canada-West Indies Agreement

I refute
that statement. I am no new-found champion of the farmers' interests. I represent a municipality in which there are a large number of farmers-
Order.

I leave it to the judgment of the House whether the hon. member has not shown 'himself to-night a champion of the farmers' interests. Is he not championing the interests of the farmers of Ontario in favouring protection?
Mr. ARMSTRONG (Lambton). Yes, and I am prou4 of it.

I am living in the centre of a sugar beet district where the people have been growing beets for years, and this is the first time I have ever heard the suggestion that the government of this country did wrong when they reduced the tariff on raw material of sugar as they did a few years ago. We farmers are neither narrow nor circumscribed in our opinions. Let me tell the House that the agricultural production of this country as a whole amounted in 1923 to $1,342,000,000, of which we exported over [DOT]'$543,000,000 worth. The farmers know that, ..and they also know that in order to dispose [DOT]of their products they must export a very Harge proportion of them. They know, further, that the price obtainable for that exportable surplus regulates the price obtained at home. In view of all these facts the most superficial observer ought to realize that a 100 per cent duty would not increase the price of a domestic product at home. We must look at these questions from a national and not from any sectional point of view. Surely everyone knows that when there is a large exportable surplus a high duty cannot possibly have the effect of increasing the home price of that product. The farmers have therefore, come to realize as a class that the arguments adduced by our friends on the opposite side, for the purpose of proving that a high tariff on agricultural products will benefit them, are simply a blind, and the plea for higher duties on vegetables and small fruits is merely a lure to commit the Canadian farmer to a policy of sky-high protection in order to benefit some other class. Arguments such as these are only sectional, and no government which is worthy of the name should consider any public question from such a point of view. The government must take into account the interests of the nation as a whole, and that is the standpoint from which the farmers of Canada do,

as a rule, view public questions. From that broad national point of view we realize that a system of high protection would be the worst policy which could be adopted in this Dominion.
Can hon. gentlemen opposite quote one manufacturer in this country who is a protectionist in the sense of wanting the government to impose high duties on the raw products which he requires for his own industry? Is there anyone in Canada who in that sense of the word is a protectionist? No. They all want to get everything they need for their own industries at the lowest possible prices obtainable, and quite reasonably so. But they are human, intensely human, when it comes to selling their goods. When they have anything to sell they are like the rest of us: they want the highest prices they can possibly get, even to the point of having the government jack up the tariff to such a degree as will keep out of this country foreign products similar to their own and in that way have the Canadian people at their mercy. That, Mr. Speaker, is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, that is high protection with a vengeance, Tory protection "as high as Haman's gallows." That is what we on this side of the House protest against.
And let me say this in conclusion, Sir. lit is for these reasons that I should like to see carved in bold, outstanding letters above the head of every prime minister in Canada a message that all comers for government favours could not possibly miss seeing and understanding, namely: Efficiency in business is attained by men who rely upon themselves and the ingenuity of their own resources rather than on government favours. We on this side of the House who represent a great section of the Dominion believe that our people have as good brains as the people of any other country. This being so, all we want in every line of endeavour is a fair field and no favour. Then we can meet the competition of the world.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Duff in the chair.

speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee that the resolution be considered clause by clause, or debated as a whole?

Mr. Chairman, an hour
or two ago I asked the Prime Minister if we might consider some of the clauses in the treaty when this resolution was in committee, and I understood him to say that that would be in order.

Canada-West Indies Agreement

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that is
right.

Then I have one or two
questions to address to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in connection with this matter. If he will turn to page 10, schedule A of the treaty itself, he will find at about the middle of the page this proviso to which I wish to draw his attention:
Provided that nothing herein contained shall prevent, the government of Canada from changing the rates of duty, provided the preferences granted herein are maintained.
I call his attention particularly to those last seven words, "provided the preferences granted herein are maintained." Now, one of the "preferences granted herein" is on sugar of one cent a pound. The effect of these words will be to render it impossible for parliament to reduce the duty on sugar below one cent a pound. I am not advocating for the moment that the duty should be so reduced, but I am pointing out that this form of preference, which is a specific preference rather than a percentage preference, ties the hands of parliament so that there can be no reduction below the amount fixed in this schedule; or to give effect to the treaty, Canada would be compelled to grant a bonus to the West Indies. Let me put it in a little different way. If Canada, for instance, reduced the general tariff to three-quarters of a cent a pound, we would be compelled then to pay to the West Indies a quarter of a cent a pound on all the sugar we bought from them in order to carry out the terms of the clause. That is the first point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, and to suggest, if it is too late to do it in this treaty, that in future treaties we should deal with percentage preferences rather than specific amounts.
My next point is that the benefits of this treaty may accrue as far as sugar is concerned -which perhaps is the most important in it- to the refineries on the eastern coast; they do not apply to the refinery on the western coast, which is a very large institution and supplies a considerable section of the western part of Canada-I refer to the refinery in Vancouver, B.C.-for this reason, it is exceedingly difficult, if not almost wholly impracticable, to get cargoes of sugar from that portion of the West Indies affected by this treaty, we having no steamship lines established to the Pacific coast that will call and pick up these parcels of sugar. The minister has already received some considerable correspondence on this subject, I think. I wish to suggest, not merely with the desire of extending the application of
low duties-that is not for the moment what I am speaking on,-but in order to be equitable and fair that the refinery on the Pacific coast and the people buying sugar from that refinery ought to have the privilege of securing their raw materials just as cheaply as the refineries on the eastern coast. This could be done, I think, if sugars from the Fiji Islands were admitted on the same preferential basis as cane sugars from the West Indies under this treaty. I would ask the minister: What has been the result of his investigation and thought over this question during the last few months? He will recall that I communicated with him I think on January 16, and that he had some other communications prior to that date. If the minister could tell me what has been the result of his pondering over this problem for some months, I think it would be of some ad-van lEgc.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Regarding the first point
brought up by my hon. friend, if the price of refined sugar dropped very low, there might be something in his contention, but it would have to come down very low. The preference provided under this agreement differs very materially from the preference which the government of the United Kingdom gives to the West Indies and to the British possessions producing sugar.
Regarding his second point as to the disadvantage, or rather, let us put it the other way, the advantage the eastern refiners have over the refiners on the Pacific coast, the government recognized that feature, and we are under commitment to extend to Australia, and this was done particularly to help out the sugar refiners on the Pacific coast, the advantages contained in the West India agreement when that agreement comes into force.
As regards the Fiji Islands, there is a considerable trade there. When I went to school we were taught to believe that the Fiji islanders were not very great producers, although it was said they did have a liking for the producer. There is a considerable trade developing in the islands, a trade of great importance. The capital of the Fiji Islands, Suva, is quite a good town and a growing town. They have a government house there that compares very favourably with the government houses of most of the provinces in Canada. If the colonial government of the Fiji Islands were prepared to make some additional concessions to Canada, I think we might very reasonably consider the observations made by my hon. friend to-night. But does he think with me that it is wise to see what kind of a trade we can make with the

Fiji Islands additional to the preference we now have?
We have had a pretty lengthy discussion, Mr. Chairman, of this resolution. Suppose we now let it have its first reading, or pass all the stages so that I may introduce the bill, which will give hon. gentlemen an opportunity of seeing it in detail. Then we can hold the bill over for a considerable time to give them an opportunity of studying it. I am just suggesting that, not pressing it at all. My hon. friend from Lambton had some difficulty in securing the information he desired, although I have been told that instructions were given this week to mail a copy of the agreement to every member of the House. It is just possible that among all the material that is sent to members, some may not have noted the agreement; but those were the instructions given.

I repeat, I am prepared to stay here and answer all questions, but as it is now eleven o'clock I think we might pass the first reading.

I was going to say that we might very well stop now, but before doing so, it might avoid delay if we were to point out one or two things to the minister, so that he would be in a position to deal with them when this matter comes up again. In connection with sugar, which is, of course, a very important question, as my hon. friend knows very well, what is he defining now as the degree of polarization? I really forget the commercial degree of polarization-

We have a long list of polarizations running all the way from very, very Iqw averages up to 100 per cent.

That is my own recollection. I want to point out this to my hon. friend: If in the ordinary conduct of commerce we are bringing in sugars for the purpose of refining them here, running to these degrees, there is a fairly substantial preference -I am not complaining about it at all-but the preference is substantial. When we get to 97, there is a preference w'hich is plus one cent. Then it works down to half a cent. At 96 we have exactly one cent a pound. I wonder if my hon. Mend will agree with me in this, that as the price to the
11 p.m. farmer of sugar beats in Canada is regulated having regard to the market for raws, and also having regard to sugar content, then on the ordinary basis of sugar beat production in western Canada a reduction in the duty, and therefore a reduction in the price of raws-I admit the reduction does not go to the producer, but to the refiner-automatically results in a reduction in exactly the same proportion to the beet grower. Does he agree with me, for example, that when his predecessor took his half cent a pound off raws, there was a reduction to the Ontario producer of sugar beets of 50 cents a ton? If he does not, I would like him to look into it, because it is certainly something which we ought to have no dispute about one way or the other. If I am right in this, and I think I am, the reduction in duty worked by this preference of a cent a pound will result in a reduction to the farmer on every load that he carries to the refinery of one dollar a ton. I think my hon. friend will find that is right. Mr. Chairman, I am not for one minute trying to press this unfairly or beyond where it should go. I know it affects only a comparatively small percentage of the raw sugars coming to this country; that we get most of our raw sugars from other sources, largely from Cuba. But has my hon. friend considered at all what effect that would have upon the price of sugar beets, and to what extent that will be common?
There is another thing to which I also wish to draw his attention, and that is in connection with the confectionery business. We get our cocoas very largely from British South Africa

speechtext: From the west coast.

Yes. Those
cocoas are comparatively cheap, much cheaper than the Trinidad cocoa. I understand that the cocoa question is a very live question for Trinidad, and that they have been asking for the specific concession which they have here. I have been advised by those in the manu-

Canada-West Indies Agreement
facturing business that they can use in their mix only a certain percentage of the Trinidad cocoa, and that no more Trinidad cocoa will be bought at all as a result of this preference, because this preference, although it is relatively good, would still leave the Trinidad cocoas considerably more expensive than the African cocoas, and the manufacturers would still have to have for the purpose of their mix the cheaper cocoas of Africa. That will mean additional taxation to the Canadian manufacturer on the raw material which he will still have to continue to import from Africa. I have no doubt the question has been brought to my hon. friend's attention. It is urged that some attention ought to be paid in the general tariff schedules to our production of confectionery of this kind. I just bring these points to the attention of my hon. friend.
